quotes.text: Most people think power automate is complicated, but strip away all the marketing and technical jargon and it's really just when this happens, do that.
quotes.speaker: Mirko Peters
quotes.why: Reduces Power Automate to its simplest mental model.

quotes.text: The core engine is exactly the same for all three types. The only real difference is the trigger. Automated flows use event triggers. Instant flows use manual triggers. Scheduled flows use time triggers
quotes.speaker: Mirko Peters
quotes.why: Clarifies the three flow types through a single distinguishing factor.

quotes.text: Cloudflow's work for modern services that have APIs and connectors. Desktop flows handle legacy applications, old software or anything that can't connect programmatically.
quotes.speaker: Mirko Peters
quotes.why: Gives a clear rule for choosing between cloud and desktop flows.

quotes.text: The trick is to start with one process that annoys you the most. The one you do every day where you think there has to be a better way. That's your first automation target.
quotes.speaker: Mirko Peters
quotes.why: Practical advice on where to begin with automation.

chapters.title: Your first flow in five minutes

takeaways: Every Power Automate flow is a trigger plus one or more actions, and automated, instant and scheduled flows differ only in how the trigger fires.
Hundreds of pre-built connectors let flows link Microsoft 365 apps like SharePoint, Teams and Outlook with third-party services, and custom connectors cover any system with an API.
Cloud flows run on Microsoft's servers for modern services, while desktop flows use RPA to drive legacy applications by mouse and keyboard.
hook: Repetitive tasks like copying data, forwarding approvals and sending the same emails eat hours every week. This beginner-friendly episode explains Power Automate in plain English for Microsoft 365 users, covering triggers, actions, connectors, cloud and desktop flows, and how to build your first flow in minutes without code.
